Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
              Office of Energy Projects, Division of Gas-Environment & Engineering

                                             ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT REPORT

Name of Applicant: El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC

Filing Received: July 30, 2026                                     Docket No: CP26-558-000

Type: 157.205, 157.208, 157.210 and 157.211                                                          Cost: $20.3 million

Facilities:

El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC (EPNG) proposes to construct and operate the McCloud Meter Station, and
about 5.8 miles of 16-inch-diameter natural gas pipeline lateral. The lateral would extend from pipelines Line No.
1100 and Line No. 1103 at EPNG’s existing El Paso Compressor Station and terminate at a new delivery point at
the proposed McCloud Meter Station (McCloud Lateral Project).

EPNG’s stated purpose for the project is to provide up to 167,000 dekatherms per day of firm transportation
capacity from its South Mainline System to a planned new power generation facility in El Paso County, Texas.
EPNG anticipates commencing project activities in October 2026 with an in-service date in January 2027.



Environmental Impact -- Conclusions:


              Categorical Exclusion

              Environment Not Involved

Environmental comments are attached.

                                   ENVIRONMENTAL COMMENTS

A.       Proposed Action

        On July 30, 2026, El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC (EPNG) filed a request with the
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) pursuant to Title 18 Code of
Federal Regulations, sections 157.205, 157.208, 157.210 and 157.211 under its Blanket
Certificate granted in FERC Docket No. CP82-435-000. EPNG proposes the McCloud Lateral
Project (Project) in El Paso County, Texas and Doña Ana County, New Mexico. Specifically,
EPNG seeks to construct:

     •   a new McCloud Meter Station at a proposed new power generation facility;
     •   a 5.8-mile-long, 16-inch-diameter natural gas pipeline lateral (McCloud Lateral) from
         pipelines Line No. 1100 and Line No. 1103 at EPNG’s existing El Paso Compressor
         Station to a new delivery point at the proposed McCloud Meter Station; and
     •   two hot taps on Line No. 1100 and Line No. 1103 at the existing El Paso Compressor
         Station.

        Additionally, EPNG would construct two new pig launcher/receiver stations at each end
of the proposed lateral under section 2.55(a). 1 The launcher/receiver stations would be wholly
within existing aboveground facilities for the Project; therefore, their effects are included below.

        The Project would be completed concurrently with the construction of a new power
generation facility that would primarily serve a data center that is currently under construction
near the Project site. These facilities are not under FERC’s jurisdiction. The purpose of the
Project is to meet 167,000 dekatherms/day of demand for firm natural gas transportation service.

         The general location of the Project is shown in figure 1.




1
  A “pig” is a tool that the pipeline company inserts into and pushes through the pipeline for cleaning, conducting
internal inspections, or other purposes. A launcher/receiver is where pigs are inserted/retrieved into/from the
pipeline.
 Figure 1: Project Overview Map
    A.1     Land Requirements

       EPNG would utilize about 71.6 acres of land for construction of the Project, and about
25.7 acres of land for operation of the Project. The land requirements for the Project are
summarized in table 1.

        The pipeline lateral would be constructed using a nominal 75-foot-wide right-of-way that
consists of a 30-foot-wide permanent easement and 45 feet of temporary workspace (TWS).
EPNG would use additional temporary workspace (ATWS) beyond the 75-foot construction
right-of-way width to provide extra space at road and utility crossings or alignment deflection
points. EPNG would use four existing roads as permanent access roads (PARs 1, 3, 4, and 5),
and would construct a new 65-foot-long permanent access road (PAR-2) from County Road FM
2637 to the lateral right-of-way. All Project facilities would be in El Paso County, Texas, with
the exception of one existing permanent access road (PAR) in Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

        The Project would be primarily constructed on land owned by EPNG, and would also
cross public and private lands, including those managed by the City of El Paso and El Paso
Electric Company (EPEC). EPNG would obtain easements to cross lands it does not own.

   A.2     Construction Procedures, Schedule, and Workforce

        EPNG would construct the Project using industry-standard sequential construction
trenching procedures that include: surveying and staking; clearing and grading; pipe stringing;
bending, welding and coating; trenching; lowering-in; backfilling; hydrostatic testing;
commissioning; and cleanup and restoration. Roads and some foreign utilities would be crossed
using the horizontal directional drilling (HDD) method, which is further discussed below.
Following construction, EPNG would re-establish ground contours and revegetate temporarily
affected areas.

        Construction activities would generally occur Monday through Saturday between 7:00
a.m. and 7:00 p.m. for about 3 months beginning in October 2026, and the Project would be
placed in service in January 2027. Some specialized construction activities may require
continuous work on Sundays and during nighttime hours (7:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.), such as
 hydrostatic testing activities, dewatering and drying, pipeline pullback at HDD segments, and
commissioning activities. EPNG estimates that the average workforce for the Project would
require about 45 to 50 workers, with a potential peak workforce of about 85 workers.

        The Project would be constructed in accordance with applicable regulations, including
U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) regulations in 49 CFR 192, Transportation of
Natural and Other Gas by Pipeline: Minimum Federal Safety Standards, and FERC’s
regulations in 18 CFR 380.15: Siting and Maintenance Requirements, and also in accordance
with FERC’s Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan (Plan), 2 and
Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures (Procedures). 3 In addition,
EPNG would implement the following Project-specific procedures: 4 Stormwater Pollution
Prevention Plan (SWPPP); Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure Plan (SPCCP);
Noxious and Invasive Weed Plan; Unanticipated Discovery Plan for Cultural Resources and
Human Remains; Dust Control Plan; and HDD Contingency Plan and Feasibility Assessment.
We have reviewed these plans and find them to be acceptable.

        EPNG would employ at least one field-based environmental inspector who would have
peer status with other activity inspectors. This inspector would also have stop-work authority to
ensure environmental compliance. The purpose of the environmental inspector would be to
ensure the fulfillment of the FERC Plan and Procedures, other construction plans, permits, and
regulations. The environmental inspector would accomplish this through oversight on the right-
of-way and environmental training of construction staff.

    A.3      Horizontal Directional Drilling

        EPNG proposes to use the HDD method to cross the Borderland Expressway highway,
which is currently planned for construction, and Stan Roberts Sr. Avenue. The HDD method
avoids effects on sensitive resources or infrastructure by installing the pipeline at a substantial
depth beneath the resources. A small-diameter pilot bore is completed, and then subsequent
swab passes enlarge the borehole until a pre-fabricated segment of pipeline is pulled back into
the borehole from the exit point and welded to the pipeline at either end. Pressurized drilling
mud consisting primarily of fresh water and bentonite, a non-toxic mineral, is injected into the
borehole through the drilling head to stabilize the bore walls and flush cuttings out of the
borehole into holding pits at the entry and exit points. Excess drilling fluid and cuttings would
be collected in sealed containers and transported offsite to a licensed disposal facility.

        Depending on site-specific geologic conditions and drilling practices, drilling mud can
extend beyond the immediate vicinity of the borehole along unknown preferential flow paths,
resulting in an inadvertent return of drilling mud at the land surface. During HDD operations
EPNG would monitor the drilling mud pressure for any for any unexplained reduction that may

 indicate an inadvertent return. EPNG would also monitor the boring alignment for inadvertent
returns. Should an inadvertent return of drilling mud occur to the land surface, EPNG would
implement measures such as impounding and collecting the drilling mud and cleaning the area to
limit effects on sensitive resources, in accordance with its HDD Contingency Plan and
Feasibility Assessment.
 B.           Environmental Analysis

      Based on our 5 review of the Project, the following resources are either not present or
would not be affected by the Project, and they are not discussed further:

       •     mineral and paleontological resources;
       •     wetlands and fisheries; and
       •     coastal zone management areas.

       B.1      Geology

        EPNG completed geotechnical investigations of the proposed HDD boring locations and
found that the materials were generally conducive to successful completion of the HDD borings.
Some gravel deposits are mixed with sandy sediments along the HDD alignments; however,
problematic materials can be compensated for with appropriate drilling methods, such as
modifying the rate of advancement or drilling mud pressure, and using the appropriate drilling
mud composition. EPNG also completed a hydraulic fracture analysis of the proposed HDD
borings to assess the relative risk of inadvertent returns based on the geologic materials that
would be penetrated. The analysis found that the estimated drilling mud pressure required to
stabilize the borings would not exceed the confining pressure of the surrounding materials thus
reducing the likelihood of hydraulic fracture, and that the HDD borings are technically feasible.

       Given that EPNG would follow drilling procedures and mitigation measures from the
HDD Contingency Plan and Feasibility Assessment and FERC’s Plan and Procedures, we
conclude that the Project would be unlikely to result in significant effects on the features crossed
by HDD.

             Geologic Hazards
        Geologic hazards are natural, physical conditions that can, when active, result in damage
to land or structures, or injuries to people. These include hazards that are seismic-related
(earthquakes), landslides, and soil liquefaction. Other geological hazards include ground
subsidence, landslides, and flooding. The Project occurs over the Hueco fault zone, which is a
group of faults along the eastern flank of the Franklin Mountains active within the past 750,000
years and with an aggregate slip rate less than 0.2 millimeters per year. 6 Published maps of
potential ground motion hazards indicate the Project area has a low potential for severe ground
motion and soil liquefaction. EPNG would construct the proposed facilities in accordance with
the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration’s regulations, which require
pipeline facilities to be designed to withstand expected seismic-related ground movement.
Therefore, we conclude that the potential for seismic events to affect the Project is low and not
significant.

        Ground subsidence can occur due to natural geologic or human processes, such as voids
in soluble rock (karst), underground mines, or extraction of underground fluids. No active or

6

 abandoned mines were identified in the Project area. The bedrock underlying the Project contain
carbonate rocks that are susceptible to long-term dissolution and creation of karst terrain and
sinkholes. However, no karst features were identified near the Project. If an unknown karst
feature is encountered during construction activities, EPNG would isolate the karst feature with
temporary erosion control devices (ECD) and/or a tarp covering to divert precipitation from
entering the feature. Further, equipment use and storage would be restricted near the feature
until a geotechnical engineer or licensed geoscientist was consulted to stabilize and remediate the
karst feature. Given the lack of known subsidence in the area and EPNG’s proposed mitigation
measures, we conclude that the Project would not be affected by ground subsidence. Other
geologic hazards, such as landslides or flooding, do not pose a measurable risk in the Project
area.

    B.2      Soils

        Based on soils data published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture Natural Resources
Conservation Service,7 the Project area is comprised primarily of sandy, clayey, and gravelly loam
soils with localized cemented soil deposits (caliche). No prime farmland soils occur within the Project
workspaces. To prevent or minimize soil erosion during construction activities, EPNG would follow
the FERC Plan and Procedures, which includes measures such as installing temporary or permanent
ECDs, directing runoff away from excavations and exposed soils, wetting stockpiled soils, and
minimizing stockpiling time by backfilling excavations as soon as practicable. Therefore, we
conclude that Project effects on soils would be short-term (lasting until vegetation is reestablished)
and not significant.
        No potential sources of contaminated soil or groundwater were identified within 0.25 mile of
the Project. Accidental spills of hazardous fluids such as oil, gasoline, or hydraulic fluids, could
potentially affect soils. To reduce the potential for soil contamination, EPNG would follow its
SPCCP, which includes measures to avoid or minimize the potential for accidental releases and
measures to clean up any releases. Given EPNG’s commitment to follow these measures, we
conclude that the risk of spreading contaminated media is not significant.
    B.3      Water Resources
          Groundwater

        Based on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (USEPA) publicly available database8,
there are no Sole Source Aquifers9 underlying the Project areas. No potential sources of groundwater
contamination were identified in publicly available databases. EPNG identified two City of El Paso
public water supply wells about 165 and 180 feet from the lateral pipeline centerline that are
completed to depths of 603 to 870 feet below the ground surface. The proposed construction activities
would generally involve excavation to depths less than 10 feet below the ground surface and we do

 not anticipate that groundwater would be encountered within this depth. No springs or other water
wells were identified within 150 feet of the Project workspaces.

         EPNG coordinated with the City of El Paso to establish 500-foot radius exclusion zones
around the two wells where no refueling and no overnight equipment storage or parking would occur.
EPNG would also follow its SPCCP and SWPPP to prevent spills and erosion within the exclusion
zones. If pre- and post-construction testing of the wells found they were affected by construction
activities, EPNG would coordinate with the City of El Paso to repair or replace the wells and would
arrange for a suitable temporary water supply. Given the mitigation measures that EPNG has
committed to follow to protect nearby wells and that we do not expect groundwater would be
encountered in the shallow excavations, we conclude that any effects on groundwater would be
temporary and less than significant.
       Surface Water

        EPNG would cross two ephemeral washes within ATWS-15 at about Station 215+00. The
washes are drainage features that convey water from southwest to northeast across the workspace.
They lose definition midway across the workspace, and do not drain directly into a receiving surface
water. Given that the proposed construction schedule is in the fourth quarter of 2026, the washes are
expected to remain dry during construction. EPNG would follow our Plan and Procedures during
construction and would also implement the Project-specific SWPPP if there is enough precipitation to
cause flow within the washes. Upon completion of the Project, EPNG would restore all surface
contours to pre-construction conditions. Given the generally dry nature of the washes, short duration
of construction, EPNG’s commitment to implement its SWPPP, our Plan and Procedures, and restore
the ATWS to pre-construction contours and conditions, we conclude the Project would have
temporary and not have significant effects on surface waters.
        ATWS-15 is on the inside corner of a point of inflection, and is required for parking and
staging equipment. Given that this ATWS would be within 50 feet of the ephemeral washes, should it
have water at the time of construction, it would not be constructed in accordance with section V.B.2.a
of our Procedures. EPNG did not request a modification to our Procedures to locate ATWS-15 within
50 feet of a waterbody. However, we find that siting the ATWS within 50 feet of a surface water is
acceptable under section V.B.2.a of our Procedures because EPNG would implement appropriate
setbacks for storage of hazardous materials, implement its erosion control devices to minimize any
potential sediment transport into the wash, and monitor the area in accordance with our Procedures.
       Water Use

        EPNG estimates that the Project would require about 320,000 gallons of water for
hydrostatic testing and about 400,000 gallons of water for dust suppression. Water used for the
hydrostatic testing, dust control, and restoration activities would be sourced from a local
municipal water provider. Following hydrostatic testing, EPNG would discharge the used test
water to uplands in compliance with our Procedures and all Railroad Commission of Texas
Hydrostatic Test Discharge Permit conditions. Therefore, we conclude that water used during
Project activities would not result in significant effects on water resources.
    B.4     Vegetation

        Project construction would affect about 65.0 acres of vegetated land with shrub-scrub
vegetation and 6.6 acres of land with no dominant vegetation present. Permanent effects (21.4
acres) on vegetation include removal of about 2.3 acres of shrub/scrub species for construction of
the proposed aboveground facilities and access road, and about 19 acres for construction of
permanent rights-of-way that would be maintained in accordance with the FERC Plan. Upon
Project completion, EPNG would stabilize all construction workspace with Natural Resources
Conservation Service recommended seed mix and application rates. The stabilizing vegetation
would include grass species suitable for gravelly soil. EPNG did not identify any noxious or
invasive plant species within the Project area. EPNG would implement its Project-specific
Noxious and Invasive Weed Control Plan to prevent, mitigate, and control the introduction and
spread of noxious weeds and invasive plant species during restoration.

       EPNG would restore TWS and ATWS (43.7 acres) contours in accordance with our Plan
and Procedures prior to applying the stabilizing seed mixture. Shrub-scrub vegetation restoration
would be reliant on recruitment from adjacent, undeveloped lands. The re-establishment of
shrub-scrub habitat would be considered a long term to permanent conversion of vegetation
within TWS and ATWS, depending on availability of similar vegetation at adjoining properties.
Given that EPNG would periodically maintain the permanent right-of-way, operational effects on
shrub-scrub habitat would be considered as permanent conversion.

        Given the relatively small area, linear nature of the Project, and that temporary
disturbances would be allowed to revegetate naturally, we conclude that effects on vegetation
would not be significant.

   B.5     Wildlife

        The Project area supports a variety of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and
invertebrates adapted to desert habitat. Noise, lighting, and increased human activity during
construction could reduce nearby feeding, nesting, and cover habitat. Mobile species could be
disturbed or displaced from portions of their habitats, and mortality of less mobile individuals,
such as some small mammals, reptiles, or amphibians, may occur. The Project would be
constructed concurrently with the new power generating facility and last no more 3 months.
Displaced wildlife could relocate to similar habitat west and south of the Project area. Direct
effects on wildlife within the construction workspace and nearby areas generally would be short-
term and limited to the period of construction; whereas indirect effects would be long-term and
last until revegetation is successful. Given the relatively small Project area and short duration of
construction, we conclude that effects on wildlife would be long-term (lasting until vegetation is
re-established), but it would not be significant.
    B.6      Threatened and Endangered Species, Migratory Birds

         Federal Threatened and Endangered Species

        EPNG used U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (USFWS) Information for Planning and
Consultation (IPaC) tool to identify three endangered (Penasco least chipmunk, northern
aplomado falcon, and Sacramento prickly poppy tree), four threatened (piping plover, Rufa red
knot, yellow-billed cuckoo, and Sacramento Mountain thistle), and one proposed threatened
species (monarch butterfly). According to the IPaC, the piping plover and red knot only need to
be considered for wind energy projects; therefore, these species will not be discussed further.
The Penasco least chipmunk, Sacramento prickly poppy tree, and Sacramento Mountain thistle
are only listed in New Mexico. Given the portion of the Project in New Mexico is an existing
access road, that would not require any improvements, we have determined that the Project
would have no effect on these species.

        The USFWS maintains a statewide determination key for all species within the State of
Texas. EPNG used the key to determine that the Project would have no effect on the northern
aplomado falcon, and would not likely adversely affect the yellow-billed cuckoo. The USFWS
concurred with these determinations on September 9, 2026. We agree. No further consultation
is required.

       The monarch butterfly is reliant on nectar-producing plant species for foraging adults.
Milkweed is necessary for egg laying and as a primary food source for caterpillars. No
milkweed was identified within the Project area. We conclude the Project would not jeopardize
the continued existence of monarch butterflies.

         State Threatened and Endangered Species

         EPNG used the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department’s (TPWD) Rare, Threatened, and
Endangered Species of Texas data for El Paso County, Texas to identify six state-listed
threatened and endangered species that have the potential to occur within the Project area. This
includes the southwestern willow flycatcher, white-faced ibis, speckled chub, mountain short-
horned lizard, Texas horned lizard, and Sneed’s pincushion cactus. No known occurrences of
any of the species overlap with the Project area. The Project area does not contain suitable
habitat for any state-listed species except the Texas horned lizard. EPNG would employ best
management practices to avoid and minimize effects on the Texas horned lizard. These include,
but are not limited to, imposing speed limits along access roads, keeping vehicles, equipment and
personnel within access road boundaries and permitted workspaces, installing wildlife ramps in
open trench during periods of no construction and checking for trapped wildlife prior to
construction, implementing a site-specific Noxious and Invasive Weed Plan, providing staff with
environmental training specific to the species, and employing a full time environmental inspector
that is a qualified biological monitor and permitted to handle Texas horned lizards if relocations
are necessary.

       EPNG requested comments from the TPWD on July 15, 2026. As of September 17,
2026, the TPWD has not provided comments on state-listed threatened and endangered species.
Given the relatively small area of the Project, the short construction duration, and EPNG’s
 commitment to best management practices for the species, we conclude that effects on state-
listed species would be minimal.

         Migratory Birds

        EPNG identified seven species of migratory birds that could potentially occur within the
Project area. They include the broad-tailed hummingbird, cactus wren, Cassin’s sparrow,
chestnut collared longspur, eastern meadowlark, long-billed curlew, and Virginia’s warbler.
Transient birds may occur in the Project area during construction. However, construction would
occur outside of typical migratory bird nesting. Given the relatively small area of the Project and
available habitat to the west and south, we conclude that the Project would not have population-
level effects on migratory birds, or significant effects on their habitat.

   B.7      Land Use

        The Project workspaces would affect about 65 acres of shrub/scrub land and about 6.6
acres of developed land that is primarily owned by the City of El Paso and the EPEC. Following
construction, about 21.4 acres of shrub/scrub land and about 4.3 acres of developed land would
be permanently affected by the lateral right-of-way and new aboveground facilities. However,
the shrub/scrub land within the permanent lateral right-of-way would not be converted to
developed land and would be restored to their pre-construction contours and conditions. There
are no residences or other structures not associated with existing EPNG facilities within 50 feet
of the Project workspaces, and there are no schools, churches or parks within 1 mile of the
Project. The proposed Project was routed to avoid a listed Texas Historical Commission site
adjacent to the El Paso Compressor Station. The Project would have temporary visual effects on
the public using roads near the lateral right-of-way during construction activities; however, these
effects would last only until restoration is completed and would not be significant. The proposed
new aboveground facilities would be constructed within existing industrial facilities or would be
surrounded by larger new industrial facilities; therefore, while visual effects on public using
nearby roads would be permanent, the Project facilities would contribute a de minimis amount to
those visual effects. Therefore, we conclude that effects on land use would be and permanent,
but minor.

   B.8      Cultural Resources

        EPNG submitted a Phase I Identification report and a section 106 review request for the
Project to the Texas State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) and the New Mexico SHPO,
respectively. Both documents were also provided to FERC. The area of potential effect
included a 210.7-acre survey area comprised of permanent pipeline right-of-way, temporary
workspace, ATWS, route alternatives, and four existing access roads. One isolated find was
encountered; no further cultural resources are within or adjacent to the Project area.

       In a letter dated June 4, 2026, the Texas SHPO determined that the proposed Project in
Texas would have no effect on historic properties. The New Mexico SHPO also determined that
the proposed Project in New Mexico would have no effect on historic properties on June 4, 2026.
We agree.
        EPNG provided an Unanticipated Discoveries Plan for Cultural Resources and Human
Remains to address the unanticipated discovery of historic properties and human remains during
construction. We find the plan acceptable.

       B.9      Air Quality

        Project construction and operation would affect air quality in the Project area. Federal
and state air quality standards are designed to protect human health. The USEPA has developed
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for criteria air pollutants, such as oxides of
nitrogen (NOx), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and inhalable particulate matter
(PM2.5 and PM10). PM2.5 includes particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to
2.5 micrometers, and PM10 includes particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to
10 micrometers. The NAAQS were set at levels the USEPA believes are necessary to protect
human health and welfare. Volatile organic compounds (VOC) are regulated by the USEPA
mostly to prevent the formation of ozone, a constituent of photochemical smog. Many VOCs
form ground-level ozone by reacting with sources of oxygen molecules such as NOx in the
atmosphere in the presence of sunlight. NOx and VOC are referred to as ozone precursors.
Hazardous air pollutants (HAP) are also emitted during fossil fuel combustion and are suspected
or known to cause serious human health effects or adverse environmental effects.

        The term “greenhouse gases” (GHG) refers to the gases and aerosols that occur in the
atmosphere both naturally and as a result of human activities, such as the burning of fossil fuels.
GHG produced by fossil-fuel combustion are primarily carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4),
and nitrous oxide (N2O). GHG’s status as a pollutant is not related to toxicity, as they are non-
hazardous to health at normal ambient concentrations, but due to their ability to absorb infrared
radiation. GHG emissions are typically disclosed as carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2e). 10

             Air Regulatory Requirements

       The Clean Air Act is the basic federal statute governing air pollution in the United States.
We have reviewed the following federal requirements and determined that they are not
applicable to the proposed Project:

       •     New Source Review;
       •     Title V;
       •     New Source Performance Standards;
       •     National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants;
       •     Greenhouse Gas Reporting Rule; and
       •     General Conformity.

       Part of El Paso County near Sunland Park is classified as marginal nonattainment for 8-
hour ozone (2015); El Paso County is classified as moderate nonattainment for PM10 (1987), and
attainment/unclassified for all other criteria pollutants. The Project’s potential to emit


10
     CO2e is calculated by using the global warming potential of CO2 (1), CH4 (28), and N2O (265).
 operational emissions of PM10 do not exceed the General Conformity de minimis threshold of
100 tons per year; therefore, a General Conformity Determination is not required.

        State Regulations

        EPNG would comply with all Texas state air regulations applicable to the Project under
Title 30 of the Texas Administrative Code (TAC). State regulations applicable to the McCloud
Meter Station include:

    •   30 TAC Chapter 111, Subchapter A for Visible Emissions controls;
    •   30 TAC Chapter 115, Subchapter B for VOC vent gas controls; and
    •   30 TAC Chapter 106 & Chapter 116 for air permitting.

        Construction Emissions

        During construction, a temporary reduction in ambient air quality may result from criteria
pollutant emissions and fugitive dust generated by construction equipment. To minimize

   B.10     Noise

         Noise is defined as sound with intensity greater than the ambient or background sound
pressure level. Project construction and operation would affect local noise levels. The EPA has
indicated that a day-night noise level (Ldn) of 55 decibels on the A-weighted scale (dBA) protects
the public from indoor and outdoor activity interference. We have adopted this criterion and use
it to evaluate the potential noise effects from the proposed Project at noise sensitive areas (NSA).
EPNG identified 94 NSAs within 0.5 mile of the McCloud Meter Station (figure 2) and did not
identify any NSAs within 0.5 mile of the proposed HDD entry and exit.

                  Figure 2: NSAs Within 0.5 Mile of the Proposed McCloud Meter Station
         Construction Noise

       General construction activities would occur from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., Monday through
Saturday, for approximately three months. Construction work would not be conducted during
non-daylight hours, except in limited cases for specific construction activities, such as HDD and
hydrostatic testing. Temporary noise effects associated with construction activities would
primarily result from the use of heavy construction equipment and machinery. Noise levels
would vary throughout construction depending on the phase of work.

       Due to the temporary nature of construction activities, which would be limited to daytime
hours with possible exceptions for specific construction activities, and the fact that there are no
NSAs within 0.5 mile of HDD activities (where pullback activities could occur at night), we
conclude that the Project would not have a significant effect on local noise during construction.

C.      Staff’s Conclusion

        Based on this environmental analysis, Commission staff has determined that approval of the
proposed Project, as described, would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the
quality of the human environment. EPNG would conduct the Project activities consistent with the
requirements of sections 157.205, 157.208, and 157.210 of the Commission’s regulations. EPNG
would conduct the Project activities in compliance with the requirements under section 157.211(a)(2)
of the Commission’s regulations.
